synopsis: ROC and DET curves show the trade-off between detector misses and false alarms as sensitivity changes; Chapter 9 and the glossary describe operating-point selection as a simple, transparent, standard detector-tuning method [f12849, f7303, f12850]. Its appropriate scope is the perception-layer detector threshold alone: it ignores closed-loop timing and braking and serves a single objective, rather than validating the automatic brake as a whole [f6980, f7302, f7304, f12851]. The recommended procedure is to select the operating point on a validation split and then perform closed-loop evaluation, with Chapter 9 identifying moderate over-fitting risk [f7305, f12852, f14426]. For automatic braking, misses and false alarms have very different costs, the appropriate operating point depends on speed, zone and task, and constant alarms can cause operator rejection; false alarms should therefore be measured per hour or per maneuver [f12855, f12854, f12853]. The booklet consequently treats detector curves as one input to multi-objective tuning under hard safety constraints, while noting that the evidence for operating-point tuning is generic machine learning evidence, with no specific off-road evidence identified [f12856, f7306].
